title: Polytopic Sieving: Practical Low-Data Key-Recovery Attacks on Reduced-Round AES
abstract:
Minimizing the data complexity required to recover the secret key of reduced-round block ciphers is a fundamental problem in symmetric cryptanalysis. Here, we introduce Polytopic Sieving, a data-efficient key-recovery framework and apply it to reduced-round AES. By characterizing the algebraic dependencies of anchor bytes (the reference state values that govern differential transitions across S-boxes), we show that cross-column and cross-row geometric consistency substantially restricts the realizable subkey space.

We apply this framework to 4-round AES to achieve a practical key recovery using only 3 chosen plaintexts in $2^{40}$ time complexity or 4 chosen plaintexts in less than 
$2^{34}$ time complexity. This sets a new benchmark for data efficiency of polytopic attacks, and outperforms other recent techniques such as Subspace Trail Cryptanalysis and Mixture-Integral attacks on very low data targets. Furthermore, we extend our framework to a 5-round attack which requires only 10 plaintexts. By pairing our sieving with a dissected meet-in-the-middle approach, we can reduce both the data and time complexity over the previously best known polytopic attacks.
These results establish the lowest data requirements known to date for practical key recovery on 4-round AES.

       Abstract. Minimizing the data complexity required to recover the secret
       key of reduced-round block ciphers is a fundamental problem in symmetric
       cryptanalysis. Here, we introduce Polytopic Sieving, a data-efficient key-
       recovery framework and apply it to reduced-round AES. By characterizing
       the algebraic dependencies of anchor bytes (the reference state values that
       govern differential transitions across S-boxes), we show that cross-column
       and cross-row geometric consistency substantially restricts the realizable
       subkey space.
       We apply this framework to 4-round AES to achieve a practical key
       recovery using only 3 chosen plaintexts in 240 time complexity or 4 chosen
       plaintexts in less than 234 time complexity. This sets a new benchmark
       for data efficiency of polytopic attacks, and outperforms other recent
       techniques such as Subspace Trail Cryptanalysis and Mixture-Integral
       attacks on very low data targets. Furthermore, we extend our framework
       to a 5-round attack which requires only 10 plaintexts. By pairing our
       sieving with a dissected meet-in-the-middle approach, we can reduce both
       the data and time complexity over the previously best known polytopic
       attacks. These results establish the lowest data requirements known to
       date for practical key recovery on 4-round AES.


    Keywords: AES, Polytopic Cryptanalysis


1    Introduction

Standardized in 2001, the Advanced Encryption Standard (AES) [AES01] has
served as the benchmark for symmetric cryptography, undergoing decades of
intense scrutiny. Nonetheless, cryptanalysts continue to push the boundaries
of AES security, with several novel techniques developed in recent years that
steadily advance attacks on round-reduced variants.
    In practical adversarial settings, an attacker’s data collection capabilities are
frequently constrained. Consequently, a fundamental theoretical and practical
problem in symmetric cryptanalysis is: What is the minimal data requirement to
recover the secret key of reduced-round AES, and how computationally efficient
can such ultra-low-data attacks be? We will focus on this scenario in this paper
and improve the state-of-the-art of low-data attacks on AES.
    Differential cryptanalysis [BS91] evaluates pairs of plaintexts and ciphertexts,
and has been one of the fundamental techniques to analyze block ciphers. However,
differential attacks are typically of a statistical nature and the probability of multi-
round differential characteristics is low, demanding substantial data volumes to
construct a useful distinguisher. The AES also comes with strong security bounds
against this technique. In this paper we revisit polytopic cryptanalysis, which
extends this from simple pairs to a set of plaintexts and ciphertexts with their
corresponding differences.

Our Contribution
We present the following contributions:
 – Polytopic Sieving Framework: We formalize the algebraic relationship be-
   tween reference state values (anchor bytes) and intermediate multi-difference
   trajectories across substitution-permutation networks. We show that en-
   forcing joint geometric consistency across independent state columns filters
   candidate subkeys with high probability while requiring minimal data.
 – Practical Key Recovery on 4-Round AES: We present key-recovery
   attacks against 4-round AES requiring only 3 chosen plaintexts in 240 time
   and 232 memory, or 4 chosen plaintexts in 234 time and 224 memory. This
   improves the time complexity of the previous best 3-plaintext attack by a
   factor of 229.7 and enables key recovery on a single workstation.
 – Low-Data Attack on 5-Round AES: We extend the framework to 5-
   round AES using 10 chosen plaintexts. By decomposing the 72-bit verification
   condition into four independent 16-bit functions and evaluating them via
   a 24-bit prefix meet-in-the-middle sieve, we achieve key recovery in 261.7
   5-round encryptions and 241 memory.
 – Experimental Validation: We provide full implementations of the 4-round
   attacks on a workstation, validating the theoretical filtering probabilities and
   demonstrating end-to-end key recovery in practical time.

Related Work
There has been extensive cryptanalysis of reduced-round AES and we summarize
the major cryptanalytic techniques related to our framework and contrast their
mechanics. A full comparison with other low-data attacks is given in Table 1.
    Classical differential cryptanalysis [BS91] tracks single input-output dif-
ference pairs through cipher rounds. Polytopic cryptanalysis, introduced by
Tiessen [Tie16] pushed this concept to geometric structures (s-polytopes) con-
sisting of (d + 1) texts sharing simultaneous difference relations. Tiessen applied
impossible polytopic transitions to 4-round and 5-round AES.
    In parallel with statistical differentials, algebraic and guess-and-determine
attacks treat the cipher as a structured system of non-linear equations over
F28 . Bouillaguet et al. [BDF11] developed an automated constraint satisfaction
framework to optimize guess-and-determine pathways on AES. Gilbert and


                                           2
Minier [GM00] introduced collision attacks on 7-round Rijndael by identifying a
functional property: the 3-round encryption function mapping an active input
byte to an intermediate state byte can be fully parameterized by a small number of
unknown constants. Similar algebraic dependencies were exploited in the Demirci-
Selçuk Meet-in-the-Middle (DS-MitM) framework [DS08] on 8-round AES, which
was later refined by Dunkelman, Keller, and Shamir [DKS10] via differential
enumeration, and by Derbez, Fouque, and Jean [DFJ13] using automated graph
search.
     Grassi, Rechberger, and Rønjom [GRR16] introduced subspace trail cryptanal-
ysis, which analyzes the propagation of affine subspaces through the AES round
transformations. They proved that for certain input subspaces of dimension 4, the
state after 3.5 rounds is guaranteed to belong to a specific coset of a subspace with
probability 1. This yielded a 4-round key-recovery attack using 3 chosen plaintexts
with a complexity of 269.7 operations. Grassi and Schofnegger [GS20] subsequently
formulated mixture-integral attacks, which combine integral cryptanalysis with
subspace partitions, recovering the 4-round key using 6 chosen plaintexts in 233.7
time. While mixture integrals achieve competitive time complexity, they require
structured coset query sets that cannot be compressed below 6 plaintexts.
     Meet-in-the-Middle attacks frequently face a bottleneck where the size of
the intermediate meeting state exceeds the available memory. Canteaut, Naya-
Plasencia, and Vayssière [CNV13] introduced the Sieve-in-the-Middle technique,
which replaces direct table lookups with sequential sieving steps that test in-
termediate transitions against precomputed lookup tables of valid differential
transitions. In parallel, Dinur, Dunkelman, Keller, and Shamir [DDKS12] intro-
duced the Dissection technique for solving generalized knapsack and meet-in-the-
middle problems with low memory overhead by recursively partitioning constraint
equations. Our 5-round optimized attack synthesizes these two concepts in the
multi-difference domain: we formulate an asymmetric 3-to-1 meet-in-the-middle
decomposition over 72-bit constraint vectors and employ a 24-bit dynamic prefix
filter.


2    Preliminaries

Let F28 ∼
        = F2 [x]/(x8 + x4 + x3 + x + 1) denote the standard AES Galois field. The
AES-128 block cipher operates on a 4 × 4 matrix of bytes (16 bytes = 128 bits)
and applies four sequential transformations per round:

 – SubBytes (S): An 8-bit non-linear S-box substitution applied independently
   to each byte. We define it over F28 as S(z) = L(z −1 ) ⊕ c, where z 7→ z −1
   is Galois field inversion (0−1 = 0), L is an F2 -linear 8 × 8 bit-matrix, and
   c = 0x63 is the affine constant byte.
 – ShiftRows (SR): A cyclic left-shift of row r ∈ {0, 1, 2, 3} by r byte positions.
 – MixColumns (MC): A linear diffusion layer operating independently on each
   4-byte column via multiplication by the MDS matrix M ∈ F4×4     28 .
 – AddRoundKey (ARK): Bitwise XOR with the 128-bit round subkey K r .

internal states and differences of AES during encryption:
 – SB r : The 16-byte internal state at the beginning of round r (before SubBytes).

   SB r+1 = AK r ⊕ K r .

2.2   Polytopes and Multi-Differences

Definition 1 (s-polytope). An s-polytope in Fn2 is an s-tuple of values in Fn2 .

Definition 2 (d-difference). A d-difference over Fn2 is a d-tuple of values in
Fn2 describing the relative positions of the texts of a (d + 1)-polytope from a single
reference point.

    For a (d + 1)-polytope (m0 , m1 , . . . , md ), we define the corresponding d-
difference as:
                     (m0 ⊕ m1 , m0 ⊕ m2 , . . . , m0 ⊕ md ).
We select the first text of the polytope (m0 ) as the reference text and write the
differences in the corresponding order of the remaining texts. We refer to the
reference text m0 as the anchor of the d-difference.

Example 1. Let (m0 , m1 , m2 , m3 ) be a 4-polytope in Fn2 . Then (m0 ⊕ m1 , m0 ⊕
m2 , m0 ⊕ m3 ) is the corresponding 3-difference with reference anchor m0 .

   The absolute state values of the anchor bytes at the inputs of active (non-
zero difference) S-boxes play a central role in our analysis. We define standard
variables for these active anchor bytes evaluated prior to the SubBytes layer
across sequential rounds. We denote them by xi , yi , zi , and wi for active bytes
entering round 1 (SB 1 ), round 2 (SB 2 ), round 3 (SB 3 ), and round 4 (SB 4 ),
respectively.

3.1    Key Recovery
To motivate the filtering mechanism, we recall the baseline 5-round attack of
Tiessen [Tie16]. Guessing five subkey bytes across rounds 4 and 5 determines
the difference before the S-box in the second to last round ∆SB03 . As there are
272 anchors, only 272 possible d-differences can be reached at this byte. Hence,
if we want to filter 240 key candidates, the original polytopic attack needs a
14-difference (which requires a 15-polytope) to end up with 1 key candidate per
byte (as you get a 272 /2112 = 2−40 filter).

     We filter candidate subkeys by testing whether the recovered ∆M C 3 is
reachable under any valid assignment of anchor bytes. Because each individual

     However, enforcing joint geometric consistency across all four rows provides an
efficient filter. While each row individually passes ∼ 63.2% of candidates, all four
rows must be reachable by the same Round 1 anchor byte x0 simultaneously.

immediately check whether P0,0 ⊕ K00 = x0 . If it does not match our current

candidate space to 232 valid keys overall. The remaining candidates then get

filtering, it constitutes the dominant computational cost of this step.

dominated by testing a total of 240 key candidates.


4     A 5-round attack on AES

We use a 10-polytope resulting in exactly 9 initial differences at plaintext byte 0.
As established in the 4-round sieve, the 16-byte difference state after Round 2

(x0 , y0 , y1 , y2 , y3 ).

 1. The globally shared anchor Ashared (40 bits).
 2. A local column anchor Zcolc (32 bits), spanning the four Round 3 anchors
    exclusively isolated to the column tracing to byte b.

Evaluating the multi-difference requires 40 + 32 = 72 bits of forward parameters
per column. Because our 10-polytope provides 9 differences per state byte, this
yields exactly a 72-bit target constraint (9 × 8 bits) per targeted byte.

5   Conclusion
In this work, we present improved polytopic attacks for reduced-round AES by
systematically characterizing how anchor bytes govern the propagation and reach-
ability of d-differences across non-linear S-box layers. By showing that geometric
consistency across columns drastically restricts the realizable subkey space, we
demonstrated that structural reachability can be evaluated with exceptionally
low-data requirements.
    We applied this framework to 4-round AES to achieve full key recovery using
only 3 chosen plaintexts in 240 time, or 4 chosen plaintexts in less than 234 time.
Furthermore, we extended the framework to 5-round AES in the independent-key
model using a 10-polytope. By using a combination of a Meet-in-the-Middle
dissection and a 24-bit prefix filter, we reduced the 5-round time complexity to
262 5-round AES evaluations with 241 memory.

Future Work. This framework opens several promising avenues for future research:

 – Key Bridging for 6-Round AES: Incorporating the algebraic relations
   of the AES key schedule (key bridging) would likely allow extending the
   polytopic sieve to 6-round AES-128, AES-192, and AES-256 while keeping
   data requirements exceptionally low.
 – Generalization to Other SPN Ciphers: The principle of tracking an-
   chor dependencies through non-linear layers applies broadly to substitution-
   permutation networks (SPNs). Extending polytopic sieving to lightweight
   block ciphers such as SKINNY, GIFT, and PRESENT [BJK+ 16, BPP+ 17,
   BKL+ 07] is a natural direction to obtain new low-data attacks.
 – Automated Polytopic Search Tools: Designing automated constraint-
   programming (CP) or SAT/MILP frameworks to automatically optimize
   polytope geometries, anchor partition cuts, and dissection schedules for
   arbitrary cipher structures.

B     Data-Time-Memory Tradeoff: BFS vs DFS Evaluation

The requirement of exactly s = 10 chosen plaintexts (establishing a 10-polytope
with d = 9 differences) is not an arbitrary boundary; it mathematically defines
the algorithm’s steady-state. By examining the algorithm under both a Breadth-
First Search (Sequential) and a Depth-First Search (On-the-fly) strategy, we
rigorously prove why s = 10 is the theoretical lower bound for data complexity in
the 5-round independent-key sieve before encountering excessive dimensionality
growth.
    At any given column stage, the forward parameter space comprises 240 states
for Ashared and 232 states for Zcolc , generating 272 localized states. These are
checked against a backward table of size 240 . For a polytope with d differences,
the probability is p = 240 × (2−8 )d = 240−8d .
    We compare two traversal strategies to evaluate the columns:


B.1   Strategy 1: Sequential Breadth-First Search (BFS)

In the BFS strategy (as defined in Subsection 4.3), the algorithm evaluates a
column, stores all surviving candidates in an intermediate list Si , and expands
them in the next column by iterating the subsequent 232 states of Zcolc . The
number of evaluations at step i is Ni = Si−1 × 232 , and the subsequent list size
becomes Si = Ni × p.

 – At s = 10 (d = 9): The filter p = 2−32 . The geometric expansion rate
   (232 ) exactly offsets the filter probability (2−32 ). Thus, Si remains pinned at
   240 elements across all columns. This is the constant steady-state, yielding
   ≈ O(274 ) time and trivial memory overhead (≈ O(240 ) storage).
 – At s < 10: The filter weakens. For s = 9 (d = 8, p = 2−24 ), the list grows by
   a factor of 28 per column. By Column 3, storing the intermediate parameter
   combinations requires 264 elements. Upon resolving the final 4th column to
   extract the remaining key variables, the list geometrically expands to 272
   elements, violating practical memory bounds. For s = 7, this cascade extends
   to 2144 time and 2136 terminal memory elements.

B.2     Strategy 2: On-the-fly Depth-First Search (DFS)

To circumvent the memory scaling of BFS, we can evaluate the same search as
DFS. In DFS, we fix a single 40-bit Ashared root and evaluate all four columns
independently on-the-fly, retaining no large intermediate sets. For a fixed Ashared ,
the expected number of valid, surviving backward keys per column is m =
232 × 240 × (2−8 )d = 272−8d . Because the columns are structurally independent
parameters, forming a valid 128-bit key candidate for terminal verification requires
assembling every combination of these column branches. Thus, for each Ashared ,
we must perform m4 trial encryptions. Total verification time across the global
loop is 240 × m4 .
 – At s = 10 (d = 9): The number of surviving keys per column is m =
   272−72 = 1. The combinations per Ashared collapse to 14 = 1. Total verification
   operations are 240 × 1 = 240 , rendering the verification phase hidden beneath
   the dominant O(262 ) (5-round AES equivalent) sieving time.
 – At s < 10: The memory overhead is mitigated, but the time complexity
   shifts significantly to the terminal verification phase. For s = 9 (m = 28 ),
   total verification tests rise to 240 × (28 )4 = 272 trial encryptions. For s = 7
   (m = 224 ), verifying the false positive combinations necessitates 2136 trial
   encryptions, exceeding the O(2128 ) exhaustive bound.
